# Integer tails of stationary oblique sections, and exact sweep identities

This note uses the proved scalar theorem in
`candidate 821242aee5d2f3e1`. Its conclusions concern one
integer variable and ordinary mixed volume. They do not establish OC.

For an integer r>=1 write gamma_r=(r/(r+1))^r. All fiber Lebesgue and
Hausdorff measures below have their usual Euclidean normalization.

## 1. A section-tail theorem with the actual coarea measure

Let d>=2, let C be a convex body in R x R^d, and write K_z=C_z. Let
I_+={z in Z: |K_z|_d>0}. Fix an integer m in I_+ and x_0 in int K_m.
Let a be real and u in R^d be nonzero. Put

 L(z,x)=a(z-m)+u.(x-x_0),
 H={L>=0},
 Q_z=K_z intersect {L=0},
 s_z=H_(d-1)(Q_z),                           (1)

where s_z is set to zero when z is not in I_+. Suppose the cap is
regular in the following precise sense:

 H_(d-1)(Q_z intersect boundary K_z)=0
                         for every z in I_+. (2)

Suppose also its mixed cap volume is stationary as a function of the
full ambient normal through (m,x_0). Then s=sum_z s_z>0 and

 sum_z s_z(z-m)=0,
 sum_(z in I_+) integral_(Q_z) (x-x_0) dH_(d-1)(x)=0. (3)

In particular the following two closed integer-side section bounds hold:

 sum_(z<=m) s_z >= gamma_d s,
 sum_(z>=m) s_z >= gamma_d s.                (4)

The derivative coarea measure assigns weight s_z/|u| to fiber z.
Dividing every term in (3)-(4) by |u| therefore gives exactly the same
assertions for the measure occurring in the cap derivative. There is
no additional factor involving the integer normal a.

### Proof of the geometry and the measure statements

First-variation formula (3) follows directly from moving a graph of the
cut in the u direction. The full differential is

 D mu(H)[delta a,delta u]
   = (1/|u|) sum_(z in I_+) integral_(Q_z)
        [delta a(z-m)+delta u.(x-x_0)] dH_(d-1). (5)

Condition (2) removes, up to zero (d-1)-measure, the graph points where
the moving cut agrees with an interval endpoint of a fiber. Fubini and
dominated convergence justify (5); compactness gives a uniform bound
on the moving graph. Thus full-normal stationarity gives (3). The same
conclusion follows from stationarity after fixing |u|: the integer
variation gives the first identity, tangent continuous variations make
the second moment parallel to u, and integrating L=0 makes it orthogonal
to u. The central section is proper, so s_m>0.

Choose e=u/|u| and an isometry Q:R^(d-1)->u-perp. The affine map

 (z,xi) -> (z, x_0-a(z-m)e/|u|+Q xi)          (6)

parametrizes the plane L=0. Each fixed-z restriction is an isometry.
The inverse image D of C in this plane is convex. Its fibers D_z
therefore obey, by Brunn-Minkowski,

 |D_((1-t)z+t w)|_(d-1)^(1/(d-1))
 >=(1-t)|D_z|_(d-1)^(1/(d-1))
       +t|D_w|_(d-1)^(1/(d-1)).              (7)

This inequality is used on the interval where the section fibers have
positive volume. Since C contains points on both sides of L=0 (already
in K_m), its relative section is full-dimensional in the plane: mix
those two points slightly with an ambient interior point of C, then
join the resulting interior points of opposite sign. Thus D has
dimension d and its positive (d-1)-volume fibers form an interval,
possibly including either endpoint.

Likewise the real indices z for which K_z has positive d-volume form
an interval, possibly including endpoints. Indeed every index strictly
between the extreme projection values has a fiber with interior, by
joining an ambient interior point to a point on the appropriate side.
Consequently deleting all indices outside I_+ merely truncates the
positive discrete section support; it creates no internal gap. The
remaining positive s_z have consecutive integer indices and concave
(d-1)th roots by (7). Their weighted mean is the integer m by (3).

The scalar integer-mean theorem, with exponent d-1, now gives the two
closed tails at least

 ((d-1+1)/(d-1+2))^(d-1+1)=gamma_d.

This proves (4). Notice that (6) has an ambient d-dimensional plane
Jacobian sqrt(1+a^2/|u|^2), but that Jacobian is irrelevant to the
mixed (d-1)-measure: its restrictions to fixed integer fibers are
isometries. Formula (5) has the continuous coarea factor 1/|u|.

### Zero fibers and boundary contacts

The measure in (4) excludes all original fibers of zero d-volume.
Such a fiber can have positive (d-1)-section measure and is not part of
the cap derivative. The one-integer-variable interval argument above
justifies this deletion without changing the root-concavity hypothesis.
It does not identify this derivative measure with the full intrinsic
measure of the section.

Supporting facets of positive (d-1)-measure are excluded by (2). At a
nonsmooth minimum the gradient may instead contain arbitrary consistent
subdensities on those facets. Such modified fiber masses need not have
concave roots, so (4) has not been asserted for those effective traces.
Closed integer halfspaces in (4) both include the entire central fiber;
its mass is retained in both inequalities.

### Sharpness under stationarity

The constant gamma_d is sharp for this section statement even with
regularity (2), although no assertion of a minimizing normal is made
for this sharpness family. Put r=d-1 and choose the finite sequence
of scalar sharpness examples s_j=(L-j)_+^r, j>=0, with weighted mean an
integer m; those choices of L and their limiting ratio gamma_d are
proved in `candidate 821242aee5d2f3e1`.

Let T be an r-dimensional convex body of volume one with centroid zero,
and set

 D={(z,xi): 0<=z<=L, xi in (L-z)T},
 C={(z,xi,t):(z,xi) in D, -1<=t<=1}.

Then t=0 is a regular section of every d-positive integer fiber, and
its mixed section has centroid (m,0,0). Formula (5) makes the cap
stationary in its full normal. Its integer section tails are exactly
the scalar tails s_j. If desired apply the lattice-preserving shear
t -> t-c(z-m), c!=0, to make the stationary cut genuinely oblique.

## 2. A stationary-tilt sweep has an exact torque term

Continue to assume d>=2. Fix a unit continuous direction e and use a continuous coordinate
t=e.x; an additive offset in t is immaterial. Let a=a(b) be a C^1
function on a compact interval [b_0,b_1]. Consider the cap family

 H_b={e.x+a(b)(z-m)>=b},
 V(b)=mu(H_b),
 V_-(b)=mu(H_b intersect {z<=m}),
 V_+(b)=mu(H_b intersect {z>=m}).             (8)

Suppose every cap is regular, its central section is proper, and it
is stationary with respect to its integer tilt.
Full continuous-normal stationarity is unnecessary in this section.
Write s_z(b) for its actual section masses in the positive d-volume
fibers, and put

 S=sum_z s_z,
 S_-=sum_(z<=m) s_z,  S_+=sum_(z>=m) s_z,
 T=sum_(z<m)(m-z)s_z=sum_(z>m)(z-m)s_z.       (9)

The equality defining T is precisely integer-tilt stationarity.
Then

 V'=-S,
 V_-'=-S_- -a'T,
 V_+'=-S_+ +a'T.                            (10)

Indeed each fiber threshold is b-a(b)(z-m), so its volume derivative
is -[1-a'(b)(z-m)]s_z. To justify this directly, the fixed-direction
fiber cap function is A_z(t)=integral_t^infinity f_z(s)ds, where f_z
is the bounded parallel-section volume. It is continuous at each
regular level: interior continuity follows from Brunn-Minkowski, and
at a regular supporting level the section area and its interior limit
are both zero. The latter limit also follows from compactness, since
the nearby sections lie in arbitrarily small neighborhoods of that
zero-area face after projection. The C^1 threshold
b-a(b)(z-m) therefore gives the asserted derivative by the ordinary
chain rule. Bounded sections also give absolute continuity. Summing
and using the zero first integer moment proves every sign in (10).
The section argument in part 1 only needs
that zero first integer moment, so S_-,S_+>=gamma_d S.

Define the explicitly corrected side quantities

 W_-(b)=V_-(b)+integral_(b_0)^b a'(t)T(t)dt,
 W_+(b)=V_+(b)-integral_(b_0)^b a'(t)T(t)dt. (11)

For either sign, integration gives the genuine cap-volume inequalities

 gamma_d [V(b_0)-V(b_1)]
       <= W_+(b_0)-W_+(b_1) <= V(b_0)-V(b_1),
 gamma_d [V(b_0)-V(b_1)]
       <= W_-(b_0)-W_-(b_1) <= V(b_0)-V(b_1). (12)

The upper bounds use S_+,S_-<=S. These are statements about the volumes
of actual ambient caps; the integral in (11) is the exact change caused
by moving their integer tilt. In particular it cannot simply be dropped
when a is not constant.

For a fixed tilt, the correction vanishes. Thus every slab swept out
over such an interval has at least a gamma_d fraction of its mass on
each closed integer side of m. If the same hypotheses hold almost
everywhere all the way to the final empty cap, by integration and
continuity each remaining cap itself has at least a gamma_d fraction
of its mass on each closed integer side. The usual absolute-continuity
version follows directly from bounded section volumes, so finitely many
nonregular levels do not change that conclusion.

Neither (4) nor (12) bounds V(b_0) from below by a fraction of mu(C).
They control the integer-side composition and tilt sensitivity of an
actual cap. No claim that a stationary tilt path continues through all
thresholds or has zero correction is being made.

## 3. Even optimized, fully minimizing stationary sweeps have no power concavity

Take n=1,d=2 and

 C={(z,x): |z|<=1, |x|+|z|<=2}.

Its three integer fibers are concentric disks of radii 1,2,1. Let A_r(t)
be the area of the radius-r disk above a horizontal level t, and let

 f_r(t)=2 sqrt((r^2-t^2)_+)

on |t|<=r, with f_r=0 outside. The function f_r is even and decreases
with |t|. For any t>=0 and v>=0,

 d/dv [A_1(t+v)+A_1(t-v)]
       =f_1(t-v)-f_1(t+v)>=0.

The inequality follows from |t-v|<=|t+v|. Hence optimizing the integer
tilt gives, for t>=0,

 V(t)=inf_v [A_2(t)+A_1(t+v)+A_1(t-v)]
      =A_2(t)+2A_1(t).                       (13)

For t<=0 the same endpoint sum is at least pi: reflect t to -t and
use the preceding derivative sign, or use its monotone decrease to
its limiting value pi as |v| tends to infinity. Since A_2(t)>=2pi,
the optimized total at t<=0 is at least 3pi, half the total mixed area.

Now fix y_t=(0,0,t), 0<t<1. For any continuous unit normal u, the scalar
threshold in the concentric disks is s=u.(0,t), which lies in [-t,t].
If s>=0, (13) is decreasing in s and is minimized at s=t. If s<0 its
value is at least 3pi, whereas V(t)<3pi. Thus the horizontal cap in
(13), with integer tilt zero, is a GLOBAL minimizing ambient cap through
y_t, including arbitrary oblique competitors. A closed vertical cap
containing the anchor has mass at least 5pi and cannot improve it.

All its three sections are proper for 0<t<1. Their ambient centroid is
exactly y_t: the outer section lengths are equal, and each horizontal
chord is centered over (0,t). Thus this is a smooth path of regular,
full-normal minimizing stationary cuts.

Nevertheless, as t tends to 1 from below,

 V(t) -> A_2(1)>0,
 V'(t)=-2 sqrt(4-t^2)-4 sqrt(1-t^2),
 V''(t)=2t/sqrt(4-t^2)+4t/sqrt(1-t^2) -> +infinity.

For EVERY p>0,

 (V^p)''=p V^(p-2)[V V''+(p-1)(V')^2]>0

for all t sufficiently close to 1 from below. Thus no positive power
of the tilt-optimized cap profile is universally concave, even along
regular full-normal global minima with section centroid at the anchor
at every level. A lattice-preserving continuous shear makes the same
example genuinely oblique if required. The body is centrally symmetric
and has an actual depth-one-half center at the origin; it is not an OC
counterexample.

## 4. A regular globally minimizing section need not control its cap's integer sides

There is an additional exact obstruction to integrating a one-level
section statement without the path hypotheses of section 2. Let

 C=[-1,1] x [-1,1]^2,
 y_b=(0,0,b),       0<b<1,
 H_(b,a)={x_2+a z>=b},       |a|<1-b.          (14)

The integer fibers are identical squares. All three sections are proper
horizontal intervals of length two, at heights b+a,b,b-a in fibers
-1,0,1 respectively. Hence their full ambient centroid is y_b and each
closed integer-side section mass is four out of total six.

The three cap areas are respectively

 2(1-b-a),  2(1-b),  2(1-b+a),

so the total cap mass is 6(1-b), independent of a. Moreover these are
GLOBAL minimizing ambient caps through y_b. Indeed the mixed subset

 {-1,0,1} x [-1,1] x [2b-1,1]

is centrally symmetric about y_b, is contained in C intersect the
mixed lattice, and has total mixed area 12(1-b). Reflection about y_b
implies that every closed ambient halfspace containing y_b includes
at least half that subset's mass, including vertical halfspaces with
boundary mass. Thus every such halfspace has mass at least 6(1-b),
which is exactly the value in (14).

In particular choose b=1/2 and a=-9/20. The three cap areas are
19/10,1,1/10, with total three, whereas

 mu(H_(b,a) intersect {z>=0})/mu(H_(b,a))
            =(11/10)/3=11/30<4/9=gamma_2.     (15)

This is a genuinely oblique, regular, full-normal globally minimizing
cap with its actual derivative section centered at y_b. Thus even its
sharp section-side tail inequalities do not imply the analogous
integer-side inequality for the actual cap.

The same family also shows the necessity of the torque term in a smooth
minimizing sweep. Take b in [2/5,1/2] and

 a(b)=4(b-9/20).

Then |a(b)|<=1/5<1-b, so all preceding regularity and global-minimum
statements hold throughout this closed interval. Here S=6, S_-=S_+=4,
T=2 and a'=4. Consequently

 V'=-6,       V_+'=4,       V_-'=-12.

The total minimizing cap volume decreases while its closed right-integer
part increases. This is an exact failure of the uncorrected integrated
side inequality, not a missing limiting or differentiability argument.
Neither example contradicts OC; these selected points are not claimed
to maximize depth over S.
